title: R Data Analysis Project and Final Review
subtitle: A short practical refresher followed by 20 new application questions
description: Review the ten R dashboard topics. Includes three capstone examples and exactly two fresh review questions from each of Lessons 1–10.

blocks.text: Welcome to the R final review. This lesson is intentionally shorter on new theory and longer on practical decisions. You will revisit the ten dashboard topics and answer two new application questions for each lesson, for exactly 20 questions.

Start by reading the requirement, tracing where its data comes from, and deciding what success should look like. Then test both a normal case and a boundary or failure case. A correct program should not only work once; it should behave predictably when its inputs change.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select R. Paste this snippet into the R editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.title: Capstone sample 1: R Data Analysis Project and Final Review

blocks.text: The first sample illustrates a small part of the solution. Before extending it, separate the input, the transformation, and the output. That separation makes it easier to test each part and locate defects.

A final project combines several ideas instead of treating each lesson as an isolated trick. Keep the responsibilities clear, choose data structures that match the job, and validate information at the boundary where it enters the program.

Practice direction: Open Home → Menu → Practical/Practice → select R. Paste this snippet into the R editor, run or preview it, and compare what happens. Then change one value or element and run it again so you can observe the effect. If this course is not available in the in-app runner, use a suitable compiler or interpreter for the language.

blocks.title: Capstone sample 2: R Data Analysis Project and Final Review

blocks.text: Now consider how this idea would behave with empty data, invalid input, and a larger set of records. If an operation can fail, design the response deliberately rather than showing a success message before the operation has actually succeeded.

blocks.title: Capstone sample 3: R Data Analysis Project and Final Review

blocks.text: Use the third example as a starting point, then explain how it relates to the course topic: Build a practical data-analysis project and review the major R concepts covered throughout the course.

Answer two questions from each dashboard lesson. These questions are newly written for this review and are not copied from the corresponding lesson quizzes. Read carefully: select the option that best satisfies the requirement, not merely an option that could work in a different situation.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 1 — Introduction to R Programming: A team receives a repository with no run instructions. What should the maintainer add to make a fresh setup verifiable?
options: A setup/run guide plus a minimal test or sample command.
Only a screenshot of the editor.
A statement that setup is obvious.
blocks.explanation: A reproducible setup guide helps another developer validate the project from a clean start.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A reproducible setup guide helps another developer validate the project from a clean start.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. A reproducible setup guide helps another developer validate the project from a clean start.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 1 — Introduction to R Programming: The app works after manual edits but fails when built from source. What should be compared?
options: The actual source, compiler/runtime configuration, and documented build path.
blocks.explanation: Build and runtime configuration are part of a reproducible program, not separate from it.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Build and runtime configuration are part of a reproducible program, not separate from it.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Build and runtime configuration are part of a reproducible program, not separate from it.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 2 — Variables, Data Types and Vectors: A filter in R unexpectedly retains NA values or behaves strangely. What must be handled explicitly?
options: Missing-value results in the logical condition.

blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Logical conditions containing NA require an explicit missing-data policy.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Logical conditions containing NA require an explicit missing-data policy.

options: Inspect its type, length, and missing values.

blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Type, length, and missingness determine whether a vector calculation is meaningful.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 3 — Operators and Control Flow: A branch for a premium feature is never reached. What should be investigated?
options: The size of the source file.
Whether earlier conditions already catch the input.

blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Earlier conditions can shadow a later branch if the conditions overlap or are ordered poorly.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 3 — Operators and Control Flow: A value enters from a form and controls a feature. Which approach best avoids invalid states?
options: Trust that the form never changes.
Validate the value and explicitly handle rejected inputs.
blocks.explanation: External input must be checked at the point where it becomes trusted application state.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 4 — Functions and Loops: Two features calculate eligibility differently after one rule changes. What is a better design?
options: Put the rule in a comment only.

blocks.explanation: Centralizing one business rule prevents inconsistent implementations.

blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Centralizing one business rule prevents inconsistent implementations.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 4 — Functions and Loops: A calculation’s output is needed by three later operations. Which interface is most useful?
options: Return nothing and rely on visible output.
Store the result in an unrelated global.
Return a value with a clear contract.
blocks.explanation: Returning values allows callers to compose operations without relying on printed text or hidden state.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Returning values allows callers to compose operations without relying on printed text or hidden state.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Returning values allows callers to compose operations without relying on printed text or hidden state.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 5 — Matrices, Lists and Data Frames: A rectangular dataset has columns for name and score. Which R structure is usually appropriate?
options: A factor for the entire dataset regardless of types.
blocks.explanation: A data frame aligns columns of equal length and supports different column types.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.

blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. A data frame aligns columns of equal length and supports different column types.

blocks.question: Review from Lesson 5 — Matrices, Lists and Data Frames: A matrix needs different types in different columns. What limitation should be considered?
options: Matrices always allow completely independent column types.
A matrix is the same as a database.
A matrix normally stores one atomic type, so a data frame may fit better.
blocks.explanation: R matrices are atomic structures; data frames are more suitable for heterogeneous columns.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. R matrices are atomic structures; data frames are more suitable for heterogeneous columns.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. R matrices are atomic structures; data frames are more suitable for heterogeneous columns.
